query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of titanium (around 1–2 at.%) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix will promote the in‐situ formation of fine, thermally stable Ti‐rich precipitates and oxide phases that maintain low friction and reduced wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a single FCC phase that exhibits acceptable friction and wear at room temperature but degrades at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small Ti addition (≈1–2 at.%) into the CoCrFeNi composition during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in ambient atmosphere under moderate contact loads across a temperature range from ~25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, thermally stable Ti-enriched precipitates and/or a Ti-containing oxide layer that coexists with the matrix. These phases are expected to act as barriers to plume wear and to promote the formation of a continuous, lubricious oxide film at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the precipitates refine the microstructure and contribute to strength, thereby lowering wear. At elevated temperatures, the Ti addition promotes the formation of stable, low-shear-strength oxide films (possibly in conjunction with Cr-oxides inherent in the matrix) that reduce the coefficient of friction and protect the underlying matrix against severe wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-doped alloy is predicted to maintain a lower and more stable friction coefficient and a reduced wear rate across the whole tested temperature range (25–800 °C) compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, which typically shows friction and wear degradation at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: The pure CoCrFeNi alloy exhibits rising friction coefficients and increased wear rates at elevated temperatures due to lattice disorder and insufficient high-temperature surface protection.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 25 °C to 800 °C; Load: similar to typical reciprocating sliding wear tests under moderate contact pressures; Environment: ambient (oxidative) atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: While the literature on precipitation-strengthened and oxidatively protected HEAs supports the beneficial role of minor Ti addition, the optimal Ti content and the precise balance between microstructural strengthening and oxide lubrication require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and (b) a Ti-doped CoCrFeNi alloy with approximately 1–2 at.% Ti. Process both using identical melting and thermomechanical treatments. Subject samples to reciprocating sliding wear tests under identical moderate loads in air, with tests performed at several key temperatures (room temperature, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C).
measurements: Wear rate quantification (e.g., volume or mass loss)
Microstructural and oxide layer analysis (using SEM/EDS) before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy over the entire temperature range, or if detrimental microstructural changes (e.g., unstable oxide formation) are observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
